title: The Image of the Unseen God
sum: Paul and Timothy write to a small church in the Lycus valley that Paul had never visited. They thank God for the faith and love that Epaphras' preaching produced there (1:3-8) and pray that the Colossians will be filled with the knowledge of God's will (1:9-14). Then comes the heart of the letter: a hymn-like passage about Christ, the image of the God who cannot be seen, in whom all things were created and through whom all things are reconciled (1:15-20).

The readers, once strangers, have been reconciled through Christ's death, if they hold fast (1:21-23). Paul ends the chapter with his own part in God's plan: he suffers for the church, he manages a trust from God, and he proclaims the mystery hidden for ages, 'Christ in you, the hope of glory' (1:24-29).
readings: A hymn about Christ

Many scholars read 1:15-20 as an early Christian hymn or poem, older than the letter, in two matching halves: Christ and creation (1:15-17), Christ and the new creation (1:18-20). On this reading, Paul or his coworker quotes it, perhaps adding 'the church' (1:18) and 'through the blood of his cross' (1:20), to tie its cosmic claims to the church and the cross.
Paul's own prose

Others see no evidence of a source: the passage is elevated prose by the letter's author, written for this letter, whose words return in chapter 2 (fullness, rulers and authorities, head, body). On this reading the 'hymn' is a summary of what the whole letter argues.
Wisdom language

Jewish and Christian readers note that what is said of Christ here was said of Wisdom: she was with God at creation (Proverbs 8:22-31), she is 'an image of his goodness' (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). The passage takes the highest language Judaism had for God's own presence in the world and gives it to Jesus, while claiming more: all things were made 'for him'.

views.H: A small church in a declining Phrygian town, founded by Epaphras during Paul's years at Ephesus (Acts 19:10). Laodicea and Hierapolis were close by. The readers were mostly Gentiles ('among the Gentiles', 1:27; 'once strangers', 1:21). Paul writes as a prisoner, perhaps in Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea.
views.C: The authorship question starts here: the long sentences of 1:9-20, the high claims of the hymn, and the idea of the church as the body whose head is Christ are counted by many critical scholars as signs of a later hand. The hymn's possible prehistory (a pre-Christian or pre-Pauline poem, perhaps edited) is much debated; there is no consensus on its exact shape.
views.L: The hymn has two strophes framed by 'firstborn' (1:15, 18) and filled with 'all things' (ta panta, eight times in 1:16-20 in various forms). Thanksgiving (1:3-8) and prayer (1:9-14) follow the pattern of Paul's letters, and the prayer runs into the hymn without a break.
views.J: Image (Genesis 1:26-27), firstborn (Exodus 4:22; Psalm 89:27), beginning (Proverbs 8:22), the lot of the saints (Joshua's land), rescue into a kingdom (Exodus) and the dwelling of God's fullness (Psalm 68:16) are all Jewish categories. Jewish readers have asked whether the hymn's language still fits the confession that God is one; Christian readers from Nicaea on have held that it does, because Christ is not a second god but the one God's image.
views.T: Arius read 'firstborn of all creation' as 'first created'; Athanasius answered that 'firstborn' is said 'because of brethren', and the Council of Nicaea (325) confessed the Son 'begotten not made'. The Nicene churches have read 1:15-20 as a confession of Christ's deity ever since. Catholic teaching draws on 1:24 for the meaning of suffering (Salvifici Doloris, 1984); Chrysostom read the same verse as Christ himself suffering in Paul, and Calvin, quoting Augustine, denied that any martyr's blood is shed for the forgiveness of sins.

deep.h: The hymn of 1:15-20, line by line
deep.b:
The passage sets two halves side by side:

Christ and the first creation (1:15-17). He is the image of the unseen God, the firstborn of all creation, because in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, seen and unseen, including every rank of power. Through him and for him all things were made. He is before all things, and in him they hold together.

Christ and the new creation (1:18-20). He is the head of the body, the church, the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he would be first in all things, because in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things, making peace through the blood of his cross.

Each half begins 'He is ... firstborn', each gives a reason with 'because in him', and each ends with 'all things' and 'through him'. The words 'heaven and earth' appear in both halves, in reverse order. Scholars disagree on whether the hymn was written before the letter, on whether 'the church' and 'the blood of his cross' were added to it, and on how to divide its lines.

deep.h: Firstborn: the history of a word
deep.b:
In Israel the firstborn son received a double share and the father's place (Deuteronomy 21:17), and God claimed every firstborn (Exodus 13:2). The word came to mean rank: Israel is God's 'firstborn' (Exodus 4:22), and the king is made 'firstborn' (Psalm 89:27), though neither was born first. In the New Testament Jesus is Mary's firstborn (Luke 2:7), 'the firstborn among many brothers' (Romans 8:29), 'the firstborn of the dead' (Revelation 1:5).

In the 300s the word stood at the center of the Arian controversy. Arius and his followers held that the Son was the first and highest of God's creatures, citing this verse with Proverbs 8:22. Athanasius replied that 'only-begotten' is said because the Son has no brothers in his divine birth, and 'firstborn' because of his brothers in the creation he joined, and that the next words, 'in him all things were created', put him outside the creation (Orations against the Arians 2.62-64). Jehovah's Witnesses today read the verse with Arius' sense and translate 1:16-17 'all other things'.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the hymn answers the angels
deep.b: Colossians 1:16 lists four ranks of unseen powers, 'thrones, lordships, rulers, authorities', and says that each was made in Christ, through him and for him. Chapter 2 then warns against 'the worship of angels' (2:18) and says that Christ disarmed 'the rulers and the authorities' (2:15). I suggest that the hymn was chosen, or shaped, so that every power the readers might have been taught to approach in worship or fear appears inside the hymn as a creature. On this reading the hymn's list is not decoration but the letter's argument in advance: before Paul names the problem, the readers have already sung that the angels are Christ's creatures. This overlaps with the common scholarly view that 1:16 prepares for 2:10-18, but goes further in suggesting the list was a deliberate answer to a teaching that ranked angels. It is my reading only.

echoes: Genesis 1:26-27; Exodus 4:22; Psalm 89:27; Proverbs 8:22-31; Wisdom of Solomon 7:26; John 1:1-3; 1 Corinthians 8:6; 2 Corinthians 4:4; 2 Corinthians 5:19; Ephesians 1:7; Ephesians 1:20-23; Ephesians 2:13-16; Ephesians 3:2-9; Hebrews 1:2-3; Revelation 1:5; Revelation 3:14

settings.by: Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender
settings.to: The saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae, a mostly Gentile church in a small town of Phrygia, founded by Epaphras
settings.when: while Paul was in prison (4:3, 10, 18), perhaps in Rome (about AD 62 on the traditional view), or earlier in Ephesus or Caesarea; if the letter is by a follower, after Paul's death
settings.why: To open a letter from an apostle to a church that had never seen him (2:1), with the standard Greek letter form turned Christian: 'grace' (charis) and 'peace' (shalom). Naming Timothy adds a coworker the readers may have known of.
views: Paul wrote or dictated the letter in prison; the readers heard it read aloud in Colossae and then in Laodicea (4:16).
A disciple of Paul wrote it after his death for churches of the Pauline mission in Asia, using the names of Paul's coworkers to apply his teaching to a new situation.

settings.when: after Epaphras had reached Paul with news of the church (1:8)
settings.why: To tell the Colossians that the good news they heard from Epaphras is the same message bearing fruit all over the world, and that Epaphras is a faithful servant of Christ whom Paul stands behind: serving 'for our sake', as Paul's representative, in the reading the Plain English Translation follows, or 'for your sake' in the reading of NA28 (see the variant on 1:7). This matters because the letter is about to warn against other teachers: it first confirms what they already received.
settings.readers: A church that had never met Paul learned that the apostle knew of them, thanked God for them and stood behind their founder.

settings.why: To pray for exactly what the false teaching promised: full knowledge, wisdom and spiritual understanding, power, and a share in the heavenly inheritance. Paul says they will get these from God through what they already have in Christ: rescue from darkness, redemption and forgiveness.

settings.by: Paul, perhaps quoting an earlier Christian hymn or creed
settings.to: The church at Colossae, who may have known the words from their own worship
settings.why: To set the frame for the whole letter: every power in heaven and earth was made in Christ and for him, and all of God's fullness lives in him. Any teaching that offers more than Christ, or puts angels or elements between the believer and God, is answered in advance.
views: A hymn the church already sang
The lines were known to the readers from worship, and Paul quotes them to show that their own song already answers the new teaching.
The lines are the author's own elevated prose, composed to prepare for chapter 2.

settings.to: The Colossians, Gentiles who had been strangers to God
settings.why: To apply the hymn's cosmic peace to the readers themselves: once hostile, now reconciled through Christ's death in a real body, and to be presented holy and without blame. The condition, 'if you stay in the faith', warns them not to drift toward a different hope.

settings.to: The Colossians, and through them the Laodiceans and all who had not met Paul (2:1)
settings.when: the same, Paul writing in chains
settings.why: To present Paul's suffering and work as part of God's plan for the Gentiles, so that the readers trust his message over the smooth talk of others (2:4). The mystery once hidden is now open to all, not to a few initiates: 'Christ in you, the hope of glory'.

traditions.q: Is the Son the first and highest creature, or is he God, 'begotten not made' (1:15)?
views: The Son is eternally begotten of the Father and of one being with him. 'Firstborn of all creation' does not place him among creatures: he is called 'only-begotten' because he has no brothers in his divine birth, and 'firstborn' because of the brothers he gained by becoming man, and the next words say all things were created in him (Athanasius, Orations against the Arians 2.62-64; the Creed of Nicaea, 325).

The Catholic Church confesses the creed of Nicaea: the Son is 'begotten not made, of one substance with the Father', and the council condemned those who said 'There was when He was not'. The Catholic tradition reads Colossians 1:15 with Athanasius and the other fathers of the Nicene faith.

The Augsburg Confession holds that 'the decree of the Council of Nicaea' on the one divine essence and the three Persons 'is true and to be believed without any doubting', and it condemns the Arians by name (article 1). The Son is not a creature.

This body stands outside the historic creeds: it does not confess the Nicene Creed or the Trinity. It teaches that Jesus is God's first creation. The New World Translation's study note on 1:15 says the phrase means 'the first creation by Jehovah God', citing Revelation 3:14, and its text of 1:16-17 says 'all other things' were created through him.

traditions.q: What does it mean to 'fill up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions' (1:24)?
views: Christ's redemption is complete, yet he has opened his suffering to everyone: whoever suffers in union with Christ 'completes' by that suffering what is lacking in Christ's afflictions, for the good of his body, the church. Pope John Paul II applied the verse to every suffering Christian and to Mary (Salvifici Doloris 24-27).

John Chrysostom, a father the Orthodox Church reads as its own teacher, takes the sufferings as Christ's own: Paul 'will not have the sufferings to be his own, but His', for 'it is He Himself who suffers', and 'even after His death He is ready to be afflicted for your sakes'. Paul is like a lieutenant who 'should succeed to his wounds until the battle were brought to a close' (Homilies on Colossians 4).

Christ suffered once in his own person and now 'suffers daily in his members'; what Paul fills up are 'those sufferings which the Father hath appointed for his body', not a payment for sin. Calvin rejected the use of the verse to support indulgences and 'the treasure of the Church', and adopted Augustine's words (Tractates on John 84): 'there is no blood of any martyr that is poured out for the remission of sins' (Calvin, on Colossians 1:24).

title: Shadow and Body
sum: Paul turns to the danger. He tells the readers of his fight for them and for the Laodiceans (2:1-5), and urges them to keep walking in the Christ they received (2:6-7). Then the warning: no one is to carry them off with 'philosophy' and human tradition, because in Christ all the fullness of deity lives bodily, and in him they are made full (2:8-10). They have been circumcised without hands, buried and raised with him in baptism, forgiven; the bill of debt was nailed to the cross and the powers were paraded in defeat (2:11-15).

So no one may judge them over food, festivals, new moons or Sabbaths, which are a shadow; the body is Christ's (2:16-17). No visionary who delights in fasting and the worship of angels may rule them out (2:18-19). Having died with Christ to the elements of the world, why submit to rules like 'Do not taste'? Such rules look wise but have no power against the flesh (2:20-23).
readings: A Jewish mystical teaching

Many scholars think the teachers practiced a form of Jewish piety: Sabbaths and food laws, circumcision, fasting to prepare for visions, and the hope of entering heaven to join the angels' worship. On this reading the chapter answers Jewish or Jewish-Christian visionaries, not pagans.
A local mix

Others think the teaching mixed several things: Phrygian folk religion with its fear of spirits and use of angels for protection, local Jewish practice, and Christian faith. On this reading 'philosophy' was a homemade blend, and 'the elements of the world' were spirits.
No single heresy

Morna Hooker asked 'Were there false teachers in Colossae?' (1973), and she is cited for reading the letter as encouragement for a young church rather than an answer to a definite group of false teachers. The letter's vagueness about its opponents is then a feature, not a puzzle.

views.H: Lightfoot quotes canon 35 of a later church council at Laodicea, which forbade Christians to 'invoke angels', and Theodoret, who wrote that the 'disease' Paul denounces 'long remained in Phrygia and Pisidia' and that oratories of the archangel Michael could still be seen there. Jews lived in the region. Roman triumphs, IOUs written by hand and the umpires of the games supply Paul's pictures.
views.C: The 'already raised' of 2:12 (compare Romans 6:4-5) and the cosmic head and body are central to the authorship debate. The identity of the 'philosophy' is one of the most debated questions in the study of Paul; proposals range from Essene-like Judaism (Lightfoot) and Jewish visionary mysticism (Francis) to folk syncretism (Arnold), Epicurean philosophy (DeWitt) and no definite group of false teachers at all (Hooker).
views.L: Wordplay ties the chapter together: fullness and filled (2:9-10), stripping off (2:11, 15; 3:9), the umpire (2:18; 3:15), the body and the shadow (2:17), the head and the body (2:19). The rules of 2:21 are quoted like slogans.
views.J: The Sabbath, new moons and festivals are Israel's own sacred calendar (Hosea 2:11; 1 Chronicles 23:31). Paul calls them a shadow of what was coming, not something evil. Circumcision of the heart comes from Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6.
views.T: Reformed theology reads 2:11-12 as a link between circumcision and baptism, and so as support for baptizing infants (Heidelberg Catechism 74), and the Orthodox catechism of Philaret cites the same verses for infant baptism; Baptists answer that baptism follows faith (2:12, 'through faith'). The Augsburg Confession quotes 2:16-23 against binding human rules on consciences. Seventh-day Adventist scholars read the 'sabbaths' of 2:16 as Israel's ceremonial sabbaths, not the weekly Sabbath. The Catholic Catechism says Jesus' circumcision prefigures 'that "circumcision of Christ" which is Baptism' (527).

deep.b:
The letter never names the teachers or quotes them at length, so every reconstruction rests on reading Paul's answers backward. The clues: 'philosophy' and 'human tradition' and 'the basic elements of the world' (2:8); circumcision (2:11); food, drink, a festival, a new moon, Sabbaths (2:16); 'self-humbling', 'the worship of angels', 'the things he has seen' (2:18); 'Do not take hold! Do not taste! Do not even touch!' (2:21); 'self-chosen worship' and 'not sparing the body' (2:23).

Jewish practice with mysticism. J. B. Lightfoot (1875) saw a Jewish teaching of the Essene type combined with speculation. Fred Francis (1962) argued that 'humility' meant fasting and that 'the worship of angels' was the angels' own worship, which the visionary joined in heaven. The Dead Sea Scrolls' Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice describe the worship of angels in the heavenly temple, which shows that such hopes existed.

Folk religion and magic. Clinton Arnold (1995) argued that the teaching mixed Phrygian folk belief, local Judaism and Christianity, and that 'worship of angels' meant calling on angels for protection, as the later council of Laodicea (canon 35), quoted by Lightfoot, shows people doing.

Greek philosophy. Norman DeWitt (St Paul and Epicurus, 1954) linked 'philosophy' and 'the elements' to Epicurean thought.

No definite opponents. Morna Hooker's essay 'Were There False Teachers in Colossae?' (1973) is cited for reading the letter as encouragement for a developing church rather than a reply to one group.

deep.h: Shadow and body: the Sabbath question
deep.b:
Colossians 2:16-17 is a main New Testament text in the long Christian argument over the Sabbath. Three readings stand out. (1) The weekly Sabbath, with the festivals and new moons, belonged to the shadow and does not bind Christians, who may keep a day or not (compare Romans 14:5). The Augsburg Confession quotes this passage and says 'Scripture has abrogated the Sabbath-day', while the church set the Lord's Day for worship (article 28). (2) The Sabbath command is moral and lasting, but its day moved to the first day of the week, 'the Christian Sabbath' (Westminster Confession 21.7). (3) The 'sabbaths' of 2:16 are Israel's ceremonial sabbaths, such as the Day of Atonement and the sabbatical years, not the weekly Sabbath, which remains. Ron du Preez argued this from the Hebrew and Greek uses of the word and from Hosea 2:11, and Ángel Manuel Rodríguez, director of the Seventh-day Adventist Biblical Research Institute, wrote in review that du Preez had shown 'beyond a reasonable doubt' that Paul was not dealing with the seventh-day Sabbath here.

A Jewish reader will note that Paul does not call the Sabbath bad: a shadow is cast by something real.

echoes: Genesis 17:11; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4; Isaiah 29:13; Hosea 2:11; 1 Chronicles 23:31; Ezekiel 45:17; Psalm 110:1; Romans 6:3-11; Romans 14:1-6; Galatians 4:3-10; Ephesians 2:1-16; Ephesians 4:15-16; 2 Corinthians 2:14; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 10:1; Mark 7:1-23

settings.what: Walk in him: the fullness of Christ
settings.to: The Colossian believers, who had received the good news from Epaphras and were now hearing other teachers
settings.when: while the 'philosophy' was being urged on them (2:4, 8)
settings.why: To show that the readers already have in Christ everything the teachers offered: fullness, a true circumcision, union with Christ in death and resurrection, forgiveness, and victory over the powers. Nothing needs to be added. For Gentiles who may have been told they needed circumcision or angelic help, the message is that they lack nothing.

settings.what: Do not let anyone judge you: food, days, angels and rules
settings.to: The same church, under pressure from people who judged them for not keeping food rules and sacred days and who claimed visions
settings.why: To free the readers from others' judgment about food and holy days, and from teachers who ranked believers by fasting and visions. The rules are a shadow, or merely human, and cannot do what they claim. Whose rule is at stake: the Torah's calendar and food laws, possibly with extra ascetic rules ('Do not even touch') added by the teachers. Paul does not tell Jewish believers to stop keeping the Sabbath; he forbids anyone to judge Gentile believers by it.
views: The 'judge' was a Jewish or Jewish-Christian teacher pressing Torah observance and mystical practice on Gentile believers.
The 'judge' was part of a syncretistic group that used Jewish practices among others.
The 'judge' was a Christian who thought fasting and strict rules were the road to visions and holiness.

Yes. Infants belong to God's covenant and church as adults do, and so should receive its sign; in the Old Testament this was circumcision, which in the New Testament is replaced by baptism. The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 74) cites Colossians 2:11-13 for this.

Yes. Philaret's Longer Catechism answers that in the Old Testament infants were circumcised on the eighth day, 'but Baptism in the New Testament takes the place of circumcision; consequently infants should also be baptized', and proves the link from Colossians 2:11-12 (questions 293-294). Children are baptized 'for the faith of their parents and sponsors' (292).

Yes. Baptism 'is necessary to salvation', through it 'is offered the grace of God', and 'children are to be baptized who, being offered to God through Baptism are received into God's grace'; the Augsburg Confession condemns those who reject the baptism of children (article 9).

Yes. Infant baptism is 'an immemorial tradition of the Church' (Catechism 1252), and children are baptized soon after birth to be freed from the power of darkness (1250). The Catechism calls baptism the 'circumcision of Christ' that Jesus' own circumcision prefigured (527, citing Colossians 2:11-13).

No. Only 'those who do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ' are proper subjects of baptism, and 'immersion, or dipping of the person in water, is necessary' (Second London Confession, 1689, 29.2, 4). The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 7) calls baptism 'the immersion of a believer' and cites Colossians 2:12, which joins baptism to faith ('through faith in God's working').

traditions.q: Does Colossians 2:16-17 end the Sabbath for Christians?
views: The Sabbath is fulfilled, and Sunday has taken its place: 'for Christians its ceremonial observance replaces that of the sabbath. In Christ's Passover, Sunday fulfills the spiritual truth of the Jewish sabbath and announces man's eternal rest in God' (Catechism 2175).

Yes. The Augsburg Confession quotes Colossians 2:16 and says 'Scripture has abrogated the Sabbath-day'. The church appointed the Lord's Day so that people would know when to meet, and so that they 'might know that the keeping neither of the Sabbath nor of any other day is necessary' (article 28).

No: the Sabbath command remains, but from Christ's resurrection the day 'was changed into the first day of the week, which in Scripture is called the Lord's day', and is to be continued 'as the Christian Sabbath' (Westminster Confession 21.7).

The first day of the week is the Lord's Day, 'a Christian institution for regular observance' that commemorates the resurrection, and 'activities on the Lord's Day should be commensurate with the Christian's conscience under the Lordship of Jesus Christ'. The Baptist Faith and Message lists Colossians 2:16 among its texts (2000, article 8).

No. The weekly Sabbath remains. Ron du Preez argued that the 'sabbaths' of 2:16 are Israel's ceremonial sabbaths (the Day of Atonement, the Day of Trumpets, the sabbatical years), the same list as Hosea 2:11, and the director of the church's Biblical Research Institute, Ángel Manuel Rodríguez, wrote that du Preez had shown 'beyond a reasonable doubt' that Paul was not dealing with the seventh-day Sabbath here (Ministry, 2009).

traditions.q: May Christians honor angels and ask for their help (2:18)?
views: Yes, while worship belongs to God alone. 'In her liturgy, the Church joins with the angels to adore the thrice-holy God. She invokes their assistance', as in the funeral prayer 'May the angels lead you into Paradise' (Catechism 335); human life is 'surrounded by their watchful care and intercession' (336).

Yes. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) honors 'the holy and angelic powers' and seeks 'their intercessions', and gives images of the angels 'honourable reverence', not the worship (latreia) 'which pertains alone to the divine nature'.

Honor, but not invocation. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession grants 'that the angels pray for us' (Zechariah 1:12), but the Augsburg Confession says that 'the Scripture teaches not the invocation of saints or to ask help of saints, since it sets before us the one Christ as the Mediator' (Augsburg 21; Apology 21.8).

No. 'Religious worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; and to him alone: not to angels, saints, or any other creature' (Westminster Confession 21.2, which cites Colossians 2:18).

title: Taking Off and Putting On
sum: Since the readers were raised with Christ, they are to seek what is above, where Christ sits at God's right hand; their life is hidden with him and will be revealed in glory (3:1-4). That means putting to death what belongs to the earth: sexual sin, greed and the sins of speech (3:5-9). They have taken off the old self and put on the new, where Greek and Jew, slave and free no longer rank people, and Christ is all and in all (3:9-11).

So they are to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, forgiveness and, over all, love, letting Christ's peace decide and his word live among them in song and thanks (3:12-17). The chapter ends with the household code: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters, each addressed in turn, each placed under the Lord (3:18-4:1).
readings: A baptismal pattern

Many scholars read 3:1-17 as teaching that once went with baptism: died and raised (3:1-3), take off and put on (3:8-14), the new self in God's image (3:10). Ephesians 4:22-24 and Romans 6 and 13 share the pattern. The readers are reminded of what their baptism meant.
An answer to the visionaries

Read after chapter 2, 'seek what is above' does not mean climbing into heaven by fasting and visions. Believers are already with Christ above; the way to show it is a changed life on earth: truthful speech, forgiveness, love.
The household as mission

The household code may be read as adapting a familiar Greek form so that outsiders would see Christian households as orderly (compare 4:5), or as a quiet change of that form, since every member is addressed and every relation is placed 'in the Lord'. Some read it as both.

views.H: A Roman household included husband, wife, children and slaves under the authority of the head of the house. Aristotle called master and slave, husband and wife, father and children 'the primary and smallest parts of the household' (Politics 1.1253b). Barbarians and Scythians were the outsiders of the Greek world. Slaves made up a large part of the population of Asia's cities.
views.C: The household code (3:18-4:1) is shared with Ephesians 5:22-6:9, and Ephesians' version is longer; those who think Ephesians used Colossians take Colossians' code to be the earlier. The code's appearance in Colossians, Ephesians, 1 Peter and the Pastoral Letters, but not in Paul's undisputed letters, is part of the authorship debate.
views.L: Clothing language runs through the chapter: take off (3:8-9), put on (3:10, 12, 14). The vice lists come in fives (3:5, 8) and the virtues too (3:12). The code is built in pairs, the weaker party first, each with a reason 'in the Lord'.
views.J: 'Chosen, holy and loved' are Israel's titles (Deuteronomy 7:6-8). The right hand of God is Psalm 110:1. 'Greed is idolatry' links the first and last of the Ten Words. The list 'Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised' shows that the church still knew the difference, even as it said that in Christ the difference does not decide belonging.
views.T: Many traditions read 3:1-4 as the shape of the Christian life: dying to sin and rising to new life every day. 3:16 has guided the churches' singing, from psalms-only Reformed worship to hymn-writing traditions. Readers in every church have differed on the household code. The churches' teaching is set out on the 'Where Christians differ' cards on Ephesians 5 (headship, Ephesians 5:21-33), Ephesians 6 (slavery, Ephesians 6:5-9) and Philemon (slavery, Philemon 15-16); this page does not repeat them.

deep.b:
Colossians 3:18-4:1 is the shortest of the New Testament household codes (compare Ephesians 5:21-6:9; 1 Peter 2:18-3:7; Titus 2:1-10; 1 Timothy 2:8-15; 6:1-2). Its form is old: Aristotle began his study of household management with 'the primary and smallest parts of the household', which he named as 'master and slave, husband and wife, father and children' (Politics 1.1253b).

What it shares with Ephesians. Ephesians 5:22-6:9 has the same three pairs in the same order, and both letters speak to wives, children and slaves directly, as members of the assembly who hear the letter; both give duties to the stronger party too; both place every relation 'in the Lord'. Where the Greek matches, this site's Plain English Translation uses Ephesians' wording (3:22-23 and Ephesians 6:5-7).

How Colossians differs. It is much shorter: it has no picture of Christ and the church for husbands and wives and no quotation of Genesis 2:24, and to children it gives no quotation of the commandment to honor parents (Ephesians 6:2-3). Its word to masters asks for 'what is just and what is equal' (4:1), where Ephesians says 'Stop the threats' (Ephesians 6:9). And it puts 'There is no favoritism' in the word to slaves (3:25), where Ephesians puts it in the word to masters (Ephesians 6:9).

The code does not call for the end of slavery or of the father's rule, and readers have drawn very different conclusions from it. Philemon, carried with this letter, shows Paul asking one master to receive his slave back as a brother (Philemon 16). The churches' views are on the 'Where Christians differ' cards on Ephesians 5, Ephesians 6 and Philemon.

Paul's word is anthrōpos, 'human being'. The 'old human' and 'new human' can be read personally (my old way of life and my new one) or corporately (the old humanity of Adam and the new humanity of Christ, Romans 5:12-21; Ephesians 2:15, 'one new humanity'). In Colossians the second reading is strong, since the next verse speaks of a community where Greek and Jew, slave and free are no longer the deciding categories. The new self is 'being made new', so the change is both complete (taken off, put on) and ongoing.

echoes: Psalm 110:1; Genesis 1:26-27; Deuteronomy 7:6-8; Exodus 20:3; Exodus 20:17; Romans 6:4-11; Romans 13:12-14; Galatians 3:27-28; Ephesians 4:22-32; Ephesians 5:3-6; Ephesians 5:19-20; Ephesians 5:21-6:9; 1 Peter 2:18-3:7; Philemon 1:16

settings.what: The new life: seek what is above, take off and put on
settings.to: The church at Colossae, Gentile believers who had been baptized
settings.why: To turn the teaching of chapters 1-2 into daily life: the readers do not need visions to reach heaven, because their life is already hidden with Christ there. What shows it is how they treat one another: truthfulness, forgiveness, love, peace, shared song and thanks. The list 'Greek and Jew ... slave, free' told a mixed church that these ranks no longer decide who belongs.

settings.to: Each group in the Christian households of Colossae, in turn: wives, husbands, children, fathers, slaves, masters, all hearing the letter read in the assembly
settings.when: the same; Onesimus, a slave from Colossae, traveled with the letter (4:9)
settings.why: To show how a household that belongs to the Lord should live. Each person hears a duty, and the stronger party is limited: husbands must love, fathers must not provoke, masters must give what is just and equal, because they too have a Lord. For whom it binds and how far: Christian households in a Roman city. Whether its rules for wives and slaves are lasting commands or first-century arrangements placed under Christ is debated.
views: The code describes an order God gave for the household, in which wives submit to husbands and children obey parents; slavery is accepted as a fact of its time, not commanded.
The code took a familiar social form and began to change it by addressing everyone and placing masters and husbands under limits; its principles, not its social order, carry over.
The code helped the church live without scandal in its city (compare 4:5), so its specific rules belong to that setting.

title: Remember My Chains
sum: After a last word to masters (4:1), Paul asks for prayer: that God would open a door for the word, even while Paul is in chains (4:2-4), and that the believers would be wise toward outsiders, with gracious, seasoned speech (4:5-6). Tychicus will bring news, and with him Onesimus, 'one of you' (4:7-9).

Greetings follow from Paul's companions: Aristarchus, Mark the cousin of Barnabas, Jesus called Justus, Epaphras, Luke the beloved doctor and Demas (4:10-14). Paul greets the Laodiceans and Nympha's house church, asks that the letters be exchanged with Laodicea, sends a message to Archippus (4:15-17), and signs the letter in his own hand: 'Remember my chains' (4:18).
readings: A real letter with real people

The closing names and plans show a letter sent by a real prisoner to real churches: a courier, a slave going home, news of coworkers, a message for one man, a letter to swap with the next town. Defenders of Paul's authorship point to these ties with Philemon, a letter that is broadly accepted as Paul's.
A letter written in Paul's name

Others think a later writer used names from Philemon and Paul's circle to give the letter Paul's voice, a known practice of the time. On this reading the details are part of the letter's claim to speak for Paul to a new generation.
A letter for the network
Whoever wrote it, the instruction to exchange letters (4:16) shows Paul's letters being read beyond their first address, the first step toward a collection of Paul's letters.

views.H: Couriers carried letters by hand; Tychicus is probably the one who carried this letter, Ephesians and Philemon. Prisoners depended on friends for food and help, which is why Paul's companions matter. Laodicea and Hierapolis were near neighbors. The church met in houses such as Nympha's.
views.C: The list of names is nearly the same as in Philemon 23-24, which most scholars accept as Paul's. Those who think Colossians is by Paul see one moment in Paul's imprisonment; those who think it is later see a writer drawing on Philemon. The 'letter from Laodicea' (4:16) is one of the puzzles of the canon.
views.L: The closing follows the pattern of Paul's letters: requests for prayer, travel news, greetings from companions, greetings to others, instructions, a signature and a blessing. The last words are short and personal.
views.J: Paul names his Jewish coworkers, 'from the circumcision', and says they were a comfort. The mission to the Gentiles was carried out partly by Jews, including Paul himself, Mark and Jesus Justus.
views.T: Church tradition identified Luke 'the beloved doctor' as the author of Luke and Acts, and Mark as the author of the second Gospel. The Latin 'Epistle to the Laodiceans', claiming to be the letter of 4:16, was copied in many Latin Bibles for centuries; no church counts it as Scripture today.

deep.h: The people of 4:7-17 and the letter to Philemon
deep.b:
Colossians and Philemon share their list of names. Philemon 1-2 greets Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in Philemon's house; Philemon 23-24 sends greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke. Colossians 4:9-17 sends Onesimus home with Tychicus, sends greetings from Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus Justus, Epaphras, Luke and Demas, and has a word for Archippus. The fit is close but not exact: Aristarchus is the 'fellow captive' in Colossians, Epaphras in Philemon; Jesus Justus is only in Colossians.

Most scholars think the two letters went to Colossae together. Those who think Colossians was written later suggest its author built the list from Philemon. The site's Philemon has the other side of these names.

deep.h: The letter from Laodicea and the Epistle to the Laodiceans
deep.b:
Colossians 4:16 asks the Colossians to read 'the one from Laodicea'. Proposals: a lost letter of Paul; Ephesians, if it was a circular letter (several old manuscripts of Ephesians 1:1 lack 'in Ephesus', and Tertullian says Marcion called that letter 'to the Laodiceans'); Philemon; or a letter the Laodiceans wrote.

A short Latin 'Epistle to the Laodiceans' of about twenty verses, put together mostly from phrases of Philippians, claims to be the letter. The oldest copy is in Codex Fuldensis, a Latin New Testament written for Victor, bishop of Capua, who read and corrected it in 546 and 547. It was copied in many Latin Bibles of the West and printed in German Bibles before Luther's version appeared. Wycliffe and Purvey left it out of their English Bible, but it was soon translated in two separate English versions found in manuscripts from before the middle of the 1400s. In the East it found its way into some copies of Paul's letters by the late 700s, but the Second Council of Nicaea denounced it, and Lightfoot found no trace of it in any surviving Greek manuscript. At the Reformation, as Lightfoot puts it, Catholics and Reformers alike condemned it. No church holds it as Scripture today, so this site gives it no 'Where Christians differ' card. On this site it is listed among early Christian writings outside the canon.

echoes: Ephesians 6:18-22; Philemon 1:1-2; Philemon 1:10-16; Philemon 1:23-24; Acts 12:12; Acts 15:37-39; Acts 19:29; Acts 20:4; Acts 27:2; 2 Timothy 4:10-12; 1 Corinthians 16:21; Revelation 3:14-22; Mark 9:50

settings.why: To enlist the readers in Paul's mission by prayer and to make their own conduct a witness: neighbors who were not believers would judge the message by how believers talked and lived. The request for 'a door for the word' asks not for release but for the chance to preach, even as a prisoner.

settings.by: Paul, with greetings from his companions
settings.to: The church at Colossae, with greetings passed on to Laodicea, Nympha's house church, and Archippus
settings.when: as Tychicus and Onesimus set out with the letter
settings.why: To introduce the couriers (and give Onesimus, a slave, standing as 'one of you'), to tie the church to Paul's coworkers, to have the letters read in both towns, and to sign the letter so the readers know it is his. The message to Archippus, given in public, gives his task the church's backing.
views: The greetings and couriers show that this letter and Philemon went together, so the Colossian church heard this letter while Philemon was deciding about Onesimus.
A later writer drew the names from Philemon to place the letter in Paul's lifetime.
